title: Reconstructing substitution histories on phylogenies, with accuracy, precision, and coverage.
abstract: Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types - including insertions and deletions - within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

title: Molecular types, genetic characteristics and phylogenomic analysis of Staphylococcus aureus causing infective endocarditis.
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a leading cause of infective endocarditis (IE), yet its molecular epidemiology remains understudied. In this study, genomic data from 285 IE-associated S. aureus strains wre analyzed to inform clinical strategies. Strains were characterized by multilocus sequence typing (MLST), spa typing, and SCCmec classification. Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factors (VFs) were identified from genomic data, and phylogenetic trees were constructed. Predominant sequence types (STs) included ST45 (CC45), ST5 (CC5), ST8 (CC8), ST15 (CC15), ST30 (CC30), ST1 (CC1), and ST188 (CC1). Common spa types were t2, t8, t230, and t88. Among 46 mecA-positive strains, SCCmec IV (50%) and II (34.8%) predominated. MecA was more prevalent in ST5 and ST8 strains but less prevalent in ST45 and ST15 strains. ST45 strains lacked splA, splB, and splE, unlike other STs. ST45 and ST8 strains harbored higher numbers of ARGs, while ST15 and ST188 carried fewer ARGs. Similarly, ST5 and ST1 strains exhibited higher VF counts than ST15 and ST188 strains. Phylogenetic tree revealed that some clades dominated by a single ST contained insertions of strains from different STs, and closely related strains were primarily associated with different CC groups. Some CC1 and CC8 strains clustered together on a branch, indicating a close genetic relationship. ST5 and ST8 clones pose high ARG or VF risks and warrant targeted therapy, whereas ST15 and ST188 may represent lower-risk lineages. The prevalence of SCCmec IV highlights the contribution of community-associated MRSA to IE. Phylogenetic inconsistencies reflect adaptive evolution of S. aureus in IE.
journal: Journal of infection in developing countries

title: Genomic epidemiology reveals multiple introductions and local transmission of SARS-CoV-2 in Sudan from 2020 to 2022.
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 genomic epidemiology has been studied extensively. However, in Sudan, limited genomic analysis occurred during the pandemic of SARS-CoV-2 transmission and evolution. To address this gap, we analyzed genome sequences from 667 SARS-CoV-2 positive samples collected between May 2020 and April 2022. These data were combined with contemporaneous global SARS-CoV-2 sequences (n = 1192) to evaluate genomic relatedness and estimate transmission dynamics. The Sudan sequences fell into 37 PANGO lineages with phylogeographic analysis suggesting multiple independent introductions into the country, primarily from other African nations but also Europe, the Asia-Pacific and Middle East regions. Notably, while the Alpha and Beta variants of concern (VOCs) were detected, they appeared to have been associated with limited outbreaks in Sudan. In contrast, the Delta (n = 171, encompassing 24 estimated introduction events) and Omicron (n = 242 sequences, encompassing 76 estimated introduction events) variants exhibited substantial genetic diversity and formed localized clusters, providing evidence for sustained local transmission following their introduction. Furthermore, spike protein mutations were identified within Delta B.1.617.2 genomes, including T95I, E484K and E484Q, associated elsewhere with reduced antibody neutralization. Our study provides insight into the genomic epidemiology of SARS-CoV-2 in Sudan and highlights the importance of genomic surveillance for tracking viral evolution, introductions, and transmission dynamics. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65085-4.

title: Molecular Epidemiological Characteristics of Clinical Isolates of CRKP Resistant to Imipenem/Relebactam.
abstract: This study analyzed carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) isolates from a tertiary hospital to determine their level of resistance to imipenem/relebactam (IMR). A total of 174 CRKP clinical isolates collected between January 2023 and June 2024 were categorized, as IMR-sensitive (n = 151) or IMR-resistant (n = 23) based on broth microdilution minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). No significant differences were found in patient demographics, comorbidities, or length of hospitalization between the two groups. The resistant strains mainly originated from sputum samples (78.3%) and intensive care units. Univariate analysis showed lower resistance to amikacin, cefepime, and tobramycin, higher rmpA detection, and lower blaCTX-M, iutA, and rmpA2 detection in resistant strains (unadjusted p < 0.05); however, none remained significant after FDR correction. Both groups were predominantly ST11, with the predominant capsular types being K64 and K25. These IMR-resistant CRKP strains exhibit multidrug resistance (except to polymyxin and tigecycline) and carry multiple resistance and virulence genes, highlighting the need for enhanced surveillance.

title: Molecular Characterization, Virulence Gene Profiling and Antimicrobial Susceptibility of Pasteurella multocida Isolated From Companion Rabbits in Southwestern Iran.
abstract: Pasteurella multocida is an important opportunistic pathogen associated with respiratory and systemic diseases in rabbits. Although rabbit pasteurellosis has been extensively investigated in clinically affected animals, limited information is available regarding the molecular characteristics, virulence-associated genes and antimicrobial susceptibility of P. multocida circulating among companion-rabbit populations. This study investigated the occurrence, molecular characteristics, virulence gene profiles and antimicrobial susceptibility of P. multocida isolated from companion rabbits in southwest Iran. Nasal and oropharyngeal swabs were collected from 65 companion rabbits, including 62 animals with no apparent clinical abnormalities and three animals with concurrent clinical findings, with no recorded history of antimicrobial treatment before sampling. P. multocida was isolated using conventional bacteriological methods and confirmed by species-specific PCR targeting the kmt1 gene. Confirmed isolates were further characterized by capsular typing, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) genotyping and virulence gene profiling. Antimicrobial susceptibility was evaluated by disk diffusion under CLSI-referenced testing conditions. Because rabbit-specific clinical breakpoints for P. multocida are unavailable, individual inhibition-zone diameters were reported as the primary antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) outcomes. P. multocida was detected in 6 of 65 sampled rabbits (9.23%). Of the six PCR-positive rabbits, three were clinically asymptomatic, one had ocular and nasal discharge accompanied by respiratory signs, and two had dental malocclusion with dental abscesses. No statistically significant associations were observed between P. multocida carriage and rabbit age, sex or breed (p > 0.05). Capsular typing identified five isolates (83.3%) as capsular type A, whereas one isolate (16.7%) was non-typable. All isolates belonged to LPS genotype L2. The virulence genes sodA, sodC, exbD-tonB and nanB were detected in all isolates (100%). The genes ompH, hgbB, pfhA and nanH were detected in four isolates (66.7%), whereas ptfA, oma87, hgbA and toxA were identified in three isolates (50%). Disk-diffusion testing demonstrated variable inhibition-zone diameters among the tested antimicrobial agents. In the absence of rabbit-specific clinical breakpoints for P. multocida, these findings were reported as in vitro inhibition-zone measurements rather than rabbit-specific clinical susceptibility or resistance categories. The detection of P. multocida in both clinically asymptomatic rabbits and rabbits with concurrent clinical abnormalities highlights the heterogeneous clinical context of bacterial carriage and infection in companion rabbits. Molecular surveillance remains important for characterizing circulating strains and improving understanding of rabbit-associated P. multocida. The predominance of capsular type A and LPS genotype L2 provides baseline molecular epidemiological data for companion rabbits in southwest Iran and highlights the importance of continuous molecular surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship and One Health-based disease control strategies.

title: One health molecular epidemiology of carbapenem- and colistin-resistant Escherichia coli sequence types in humans, poultry, and the environment in Pakistan.
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is a grave One Health concern, leading to increased mortality and economic loss globally. These pathogens have acquired several resistance genes against WHO-defined medically important classes of antibiotics. Therefore, we plan to investigate AMR prevalence within the One Health framework. A total of 300 samples (100 each from human clinical, poultry, and environmental sources) were collected aseptically. We cultured isolates using standard microbiological methods and identified them with the VITEK® 2 Compact system. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Two-locus CH typing was used to assign sequence types (STs), and PCR was performed to detect blaNDM, blaVIM, blaIMP, blaOXA, and mcr-1. A total of 27 carbapenem-resistant E. coli (CR-EC) and 3 colistin-resistant E. coli (ColR-EC) isolates were recovered from human samples, 38 CR-EC and 5 ColR-EC from environmental samples, and 25 ColR-EC from poultry samples. Among all isolates, ST101 (21/90; 23.3%), ST131 (15/90; 16.7%), and ST405 (15/90; 16.7%) were the predominant sequence types. All three reservoirs harboured ST101, ST131, and ST405, while ST648 was shared between human and environmental isolates, and ST10 was shared between poultry and environmental isolates. Among environmental carbapenem-resistant isolates, blaNDM (20/38; 52.6%), blaVIM (18/38; 47.4%), blaIMP (11/38; 28.9%), blaOXA (6/38; 15.8%), and mcr-1 (5/38; 13.2%) were detected. All human carbapenem-resistant isolates carried blaNDM (27/27; 100%), whereas all poultry colistin-resistant isolates harboured mcr-1 (25/25; 100%). High-risk multidrug-resistant E. coli lineages carrying carbapenemase and colistin resistance genes are widely distributed across human, poultry, and environmental reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Emergence of canine adenovirus infection in mink from five provinces in Northern China.
abstract: Canine adenovirus 1 (CAV-1) is the causative agent of canine infectious hepatitis and fox encephalitis. However, epidemiological information regarding CAV-1 infection in mink remains limited. From September 2022 to February 2023, a total of 540 rectal swab samples from 18 mink farms from five provinces in China were collected, and viral nucleic acids were identified, sequenced, and analyzed. The overall positive rate across mink farms was 34.00%, with that of Shandong Province being the highest (67.33%). In Shandong Province, the positive rate of mink CAV-1 in Rizhao city was 100%. According to the fiber phylogenetic tree, the fiber sequences in the cities of Qinhuangdao (042803), Rizhao (042801), and Weihai (050101) were located in the same distinct branch and were different from strains isolated from other animals. These obtained fiber sequences were under purifying selection compared with the CAV-1 fiber (AC_000003.1). Compared with the fiber sequence AP_000069.1, the mutation of the 042402-TS amino acid changed the B-cell epitope and the 3D structure. However, the binding affinity between the obtained fiber sequence and the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR) was not different. These results indicate that strain 042402 exhibits notable genetic divergence in the fiber fragment compared with the strains from other host species, and the prevalence of CAV-1 has been confirmed in mink. Therefore, it is important to further clarify the evolution and molecular epidemiology of CAV-1 in mink in the future.

title: High-Fidelity Whole-Genome Sequencing of White Spot Syndrome Virus From Infected Shrimp via Iodixanol Density Gradient Centrifugation and Enzymatic Host Depletion.
abstract: White Spot Disease (WSD), caused by White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV; Whispovirus xiabaidian), inflicts catastrophic losses on global shrimp aquaculture. Characterizing strain-level virulence variations requires comparative genomics; however, the lack of continuous crustacean cell lines severely constrains direct sequencing from infected tissues due to overwhelming host DNA background. Here, we established an efficient particle purification protocol coupling iodixanol density gradient ultracentrifugation with enzymatic nuclease digestion to selectively deplete host nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. The developed protocol enriched target WSSV reads to > 70% across both Illumina MiSeq and Oxford Nanopore MinION platforms while virtually eliminating coverage bias in non-amplified libraries. Stepwise downsampling demonstrated that our reference-guided assembly pipeline reliably reconstructs complete ~300-kbp genomes from as little as 5-10 Mbp of sequencing data, enabling multiplexed sequencing at approximately $10 USD per isolate. Applying this optimized framework, we successfully resolved the complete genomes of two novel field isolates from Thailand (TH-W11) and the Philippines (PHR3-ZS-M101724, representing the first complete WSSV genome from the country), uncovering distinct phylogenetic lineages and large genomic deletions (~5.6-5.8 kbp), which were experimentally confirmed by flanking PCR. This cost-effective platform provides a standardized pipeline for high-throughput genomic surveillance and molecular epidemiology of emerging WSSV isolates.
authors: Debrah Jannsen D J N Almazan

title: Prevalence, molecular characterization, and factors associated with hemotropic Mycoplasma infection in domestic cats (Felis catus) in the semi-arid region of Paraíba, Brazil.
abstract: Hemotropic mycoplasmas are bacteria that parasitize the surface of erythrocytes and may cause clinical alterations of varying severity in felines. This study aimed to determine the prevalence, identify factors associated with infection, and molecularly characterize the circulating species in cats from the semi-arid region of Paraíba, Brazil. A total of 354 cats from the municipality of Sousa were evaluated through clinical and epidemiological assessment and blood sampling for molecular detection of 'Candidatus Mycoplasma haemominutum' (CMhm), Mycoplasma haemofelis (Mhf), and 'Candidatus Mycoplasma turicense' (CMt) by PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene. Selected samples were subjected to Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. The overall prevalence of hemotropic mycoplasmas was 36.2% (128/354), with CMhm being the most frequent (31.4%), followed by Mhf (4.8%) and CMt (3.7%); coinfection with CMhm and Mhf was observed in 3.7% of the animals. In the multivariable analysis, age over four years and the presence of lymph node abnormalities were identified as factors associated with positivity. BLASTn showed 99.72-100% sequence identity; phylogenetic analysis grouped five sequences with CMhm references and one with CMt references, while the 16S rRNA fragment could not distinguish M. haemofelis from M. haemocanis. These findings expand the knowledge of the molecular epidemiology of these agents in the semi-arid region of Paraíba and reinforce the importance of their investigation in routine diagnostics, as well as the need for further studies on their genetic diversity, transmission, and clinical relevance.
journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases

title: A computational tool to predict how new coronavirus variants evade antibody defenses.
abstract: The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants with mutations in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) poses a significant challenge to antibody-mediated immunity and ongoing vaccine effectiveness. In this work, we present RBD-Escape, a transparent and experimentally grounded computational framework for estimating how combinations of RBD mutations influence recognition by polyclonal neutralizing antibodies. The framework integrates deep mutational scanning (DMS) measurements from 33 monoclonal antibodies characterized across multiple independent studies and aggregates these data into a unified model of antibody escape. Unlike black-box predictive approaches, RBD-Escape directly leverages experimentally measured escape profiles, providing an interpretable representation of mutation-driven immune evasion. The proposed framework estimates the impact of arbitrary mutation combinations by modeling both additive and redundant antibody escape effects. Validation against independent neutralization datasets demonstrates strong agreement between predicted binding scores and experimentally measured neutralization outcomes, indicating that aggregated DMS data can effectively capture major patterns of antibody escape. Application of the framework to the Omicron variant revealed extensive predicted reductions in antibody recognition relative to earlier SARS-CoV-2 variants, consistent with its observed immune-evasive properties. In addition to quantitative escape prediction, RBD-Escape provides interactive visualization capabilities that facilitate exploration of mutation-specific and variant-level escape patterns. Although the current implementation focuses exclusively on mutations within the RBD and does not account for contributions from other spike protein regions, it offers a rapid, interpretable, and experiment-driven approach for evaluating emerging variants. The framework has potential applications in genomic surveillance, vaccine evaluation, and the assessment of mutation-driven antigenic change, but predictions should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive (Lucas et al., 2021).
